Patient Vignette: "Captain M."

Captain M. is a 55-year-old Latin American man, a retired Navy officer, who has been in a committed relationship for the past eight years. He presents with a guarded, almost formal demeanor, his back straight against the chair, his hands resting flat on his knees. He speaks in a low, deliberate voice, as if each word is a carefully chosen stone placed in a wall. He is not here for himself, he says. He is here because his partner, Elena, is "worried." He is tired of her worrying.

The story he tells begins not in the ocean, but on land. Fifteen years ago, during a period of civil unrest in a coastal city where he was stationed as a liaison officer, he was caught in a civilian evacuation zone that collapsed into chaos. He was not in uniform. He was off-duty, walking back to his quarters after a meeting, when the first mortar round hit a market two blocks away. He describes the sound not as an explosion, but as a "wrongness" in the air—a pressure that pushed against his chest before the noise arrived. He ran. He helped pull a woman from a collapsed awning. He held a child whose leg was bleeding while they waited for a transport that never came. For three days, he was a civilian in a war zone, stripped of rank and authority, just a man trying to stay alive.

He does not call it a trauma. He calls it "a bad week."

In the months that followed, he returned to his ship, to his duties. He did not speak of it. He was promoted. He was respected. But inside, a quiet erosion had begun. He started sleeping with his back to the door. He stopped drinking coffee because the smell of it—burnt and bitter—reminded him of the market. He found himself scanning rooftops during port calls, his eyes moving in a pattern he couldn't control. He did not connect these things to the "bad week." He believed he had simply become more vigilant, more professional.

Now, retired and living in a quiet suburb, the vigilance has not faded. It has calcified. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. every morning—the exact time the first mortar struck—with his heart hammering and a cold sweat on his back. He does not remember dreams, only a feeling of falling. He has mapped every exit in his home, his grocery store, his doctor's office. He cannot sit facing away from a door. Elena has learned to sit beside him, not across from him, because he flinches when she enters his line of sight unexpectedly.

His irritability is a quiet, cutting thing. He does not yell. He withdraws. When the neighbor's dog barks, he feels a spike of rage so sharp it frightens him. He has stopped attending social gatherings because the noise of multiple conversations—the overlapping voices—makes his chest tight and his vision narrow. He tells himself he just prefers solitude. He tells Elena he is "fine." He believes this, mostly.

His job as a Navy officer trained him to compartmentalize, to function under pressure, to suppress fear. That training, once his greatest strength, is now his prison. He cannot tell the difference between a real threat and a memory. His body lives in the war zone, even though his mind knows he is safe. He feels a deep, bone-level shame about this. He is a man who led others. He should not be undone by a sound, a smell, a shadow.

He is here, in this chair, because Elena said she would leave if he didn't come. He does not want to lose her. But he also does not know how to let go of the watch he has kept for fifteen years. He does not know who he would be if he stopped scanning the rooftops.
